title: A look at Sickle Cell Awareness Month - NewsBreak
text:
By Jay Lathon No media credit provided. ,
1 days ago
TEXAS ( FOX 44 ) – The genetic mutation is found in 1 and 365 African Americans and effects over 100,000 Americans each year.
Sickle Cell Anemia Disease causes the blood cells to be misshapen and create blockages in the body causing a immense pain called a “crisis” requiring hospitalization. Sickle cell diagnoses only happen what both parents carry the trait for the disease.
I spoke with Nyseya Brown, a sickle cell patient in Texas, on how the disease impacts her life. She said that she often tried to go school but when the crises frequented her monthly she became home schooled. “I can’t sprint and overheat or be too cold without sickle cell impacting me.” She also claims that making friends is hard when she can’t do all the the things that adults do because of her ailment. At only 25 years old sickle cell triggered a pulmonary embolism causing her to have a stroke.
Anna Dick a nurse practitioner at Baylor Scott and White says that a majority of the kids she sees have a relatively normal life with proper management of the body. She told me that each child born in the U.S. is tested for the genetic mutation at birth and given antibiotics but as they get older they can receive experimental medication like Hydroxyurea to minimize the replication of crescent shaped blood cells.
With no known cure for the disease both doctors and patients ask for patience and sympathy for those experiencing the issue as there is no known cure for Sickle Cell Anemia. For more information, you can click here .
